item.content:encoded:
On what American advertising must become, now that it has become the Nation's picture of itself

The Loom of the Republic

On what American advertising must become, now that it has become the Nation's picture of itself

We have, then, decided it: this Republic, once a Nation of Farmers, then a Nation of Workshops, is become, in these years of our Lord, a Nation of Advertisements. Turn it how you will, deny it who dares,— the plain arithmetic of the thing will not be argued down. More of the American's waking hour is spent under the persuading Voice than under any Pulpit, Parliament, or Schoolroom his Fathers built for him; more of the Republic's wealth is meted out to the men who make the Voice speak than to the men who dig the coal or lay the rail or teach the child his letters. Advertising is not, then, some decent adjunct trade, some mere upholstery clapped upon Commerce to help it sell its wares,— it is become, whether the Advertising Man knows it or no, the actual Loom on which the Nation's picture of itself is daily woven. Whoso sits at that Loom is not a Tradesman merely; he is, in the most fearful and literal sense, a Legislator; for what he weaves, thirty millions of eyes will look upon before they look upon anything else this day, and by that weaving will shape what they take to be desirable, possible, and true. This being granted,— and it is granted the moment you count the dollars and the hours,— the question ceases to be, "How shall Advertising sell more soap?" and becomes the older and more terrible question that every Ruling Class of every Age has had put to it, whether it would or no: "What Vision hast thou for the People thou rulest?" For Rule it is. Adam Smith's invisible hand has, in our day, hired itself a very visible mouth, and that mouth talks to the Republic more hours in the year than any Statesman, and is trusted, alas, rather better. It is idle, therefore, to go on treating Madison Avenue and its innumerable digital heirs as though they were still peddling nostrums from a cart, some harmless Yankee huckstering to be regulated a little and then forgotten. No: the Huckster's cart has become the Nation's Pulpit, without anyone's quite resolving that it should; and now, resolved or not, there it stands, and thirty millions listen to it between their breakfast and their labor. II. Well, then,— thou Huckster-Elevated-to-Pulpit, thou Salesman suddenly finding a Sceptre in thy hand where thou didst expect only a sample-case,— what wilt thou do with it? For do something with it thou must; a Sceptre held is never neutral; it either builds a Cosmos or it lets the Chaos in, there is no third estate open to it. Here is the whole burden of what I have to say to thee, and I will say it plainly, in the plainest words this old tongue commands. Thou shalt not, in the first place, go on pretending that thou art merely "moving product," as thy own Cant-phrase has it, while all the while thou art in very fact moving Desire itself,— manufacturing, in thy laboratories of persuasion, the very wants that yesterday did not exist and that tomorrow shall be spoken of by the People as needs older than their own birth. This is a godlike power, be it never so disguised in spreadsheets and click-through rates; and a godlike power exercised in a fit of absence of mind, without so much as asking what sort of Man it is making, is the very definition of that Mechanical Age I have elsewhere denounced,— the Age that builds engines of enormous force and appoints no one to ask what they are for. If, then, thou wilt hold the Sceptre honestly, hold it thus: Let the thing thou sellest be a real thing, doing a real service to a real man, and let thy Persuasion be the naming of that service in its plainest coat, not the draping of an emptiness in borrowed glories. This is not a counsel of dullness; it is a counsel of Sincerity, which, rightly used, is the most arresting weapon in any Persuader's armory,— for the world is so sated with Phantasm-selling, so wearied unto death with the sixteenth reformulated Serum of Eternal Youth, that the man who stands up in the marketplace and says a true thing plainly will, before long, be heard above all the shrieking, precisely because he is the only one not shrieking. III. And here is the second charge upon thee, harder than the first: that thou take up, consciously and with thy whole strength, the work of Vision-Making, since Vision-Making has in any case fallen into thy lap, whether asked for or no. Every civilization that has endured has had some Class charged, formally or informally, with telling the People what is admirable, what is to be striven for, what a good life among them looks like,— the Priest did it once, and the Bard, and after them the Schoolmaster and the Editor; and now, in this Advertising Republic of ours, it is thou, oftener than any of these, who paints the picture of the Good Life that the schoolboy and the tired clerk alike carry home with them at evening. Thou canst not now resign the office; the only question left thee is whether thou wilt fill it as a Hero fills a post assigned him by the Eternities, or as a Quack fills it, mumbling incantations over an empty till. Fill it, then, as a Hero would. Let the Republic's advertised Vision of itself be a Vision of Work well done, of the Craftsman honored above the mere Possessor, of Strength that serves rather than Strength that merely glitters; let it show forth Industry, Family, Neighbor-hood, the plain dignities that do not date and do not disappoint, rather than the eternal parade of Idleness-as-Paradise which is the laziest lie any Persuader ever told, and the most corrosive, since it teaches thirty millions of grown men and women, hour upon hour, that the highest good attainable is to want, acquire, and want again, forever, on a wheel that goes nowhere. A Nation schooled daily in that catechism will not, in the end, be a Nation of Workmen; it will be a Nation of Debtors, restless, dissatisfied, and secretly ashamed, not knowing quite why. IV. I hear the Advertising Man protest,— for he always protests, being by trade a most fluent creature,— that he is a Servant only, that he sells what the Client bids him

item.title: The Message in the Gap
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Marshall McLuhan)
item.description: On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers
item.content:encoded:
On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers

The Message in the Gap

On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers

The pause was never empty. It only looked empty to an industry that reads a screen for content and misses what the screen is doing while it appears to do nothing. The IAB Tech Lab has now issued a formal signaling standard for six formats — pause ads, menu ads, screensavers, in-scene placements, squeezebacks, overlays — and the trade calls this an expansion of inventory. It is not an expansion. It is a discovery. The industry has located a room in the house it has lived in for seventy years and only now noticed the door. Every medium extends a faculty and numbs one in the same motion. The pre-roll extended the interruption; it numbed the viewer's sense of a program's edges, so that ad and content blurred into a single continuous flow the viewer stopped resisting. The pause button did something else entirely. It was built to extend the viewer's control — stop the world, hold the frame — and it succeeded so completely that the industry filed the pause under leisure, under bathroom break, under the one gesture on the remote that had escaped monetization. A control extended is a market amputated. Nobody sells to a room they believe is empty. The standard says the room was never empty; someone was standing in it the whole time, waiting. Watch what the standard actually retrieves. The pause ad is not new. It is the shop window revived — the thing you look at while you are not moving, addressed to a body that has voluntarily stopped, not one interrupted mid-stride. The menu ad retrieves the door-to-door catalogue, the object placed in your hand at the threshold before you have chosen a room to enter. The screensaver retrieves the parlor wallpaper, the ornament that speaks only when no one is speaking to it. None of these formats required invention. They required a vocabulary common enough that a demand-side platform and a supply-side platform could agree they were looking at the same gap, and a gap without a shared name cannot be bought or sold; it can only be noticed, privately, by whoever happens to be looking. A standard is a ratio before it is a rule. What the Tech Lab has actually done is tell six different silences apart from one another — the silence of a held frame, the silence of a chosen menu, the silence of an idle screen — and give a machine the means to bid on each differently. The content that will fill these gaps is a decoy, as content always is; the medium's real message is that the industry's sense of where a program ends and an audience's private moment begins has just been redrawn, on a Tuesday, by a signaling spec nobody outside the trade will ever read. The screen was addressing you before it had anything to say. Now it has been given the words. — Marshall McLuhan

item.title: The Withdrawn Witness
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Thomas Carlyle)
item.description: On the Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp withdrawals from Media Rating Council audit
item.content:encoded:
On the Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp withdrawals from Media Rating Council audit

The Withdrawn Witness

On the Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp withdrawals from Media Rating Council audit

Behold two Currencies, self-proclaimed heirs of the whole vanished Kingdom of Panel-Measurement, and both of them, in this same month of July, quietly withdrawing from the one Tribunal set over them to say whether they speak truth! Not covertly did they do it,— no, with a Quarterly Update, and a press clarification, and the whole soft apparatus of Company Language; but withdraw they did; and the world of buyers, who had been told for three years that Deliverance was coming, that a true Successor to the old dead Panel-God was at hand, must now digest the plain fact: the two Successors most spoken of have both, at the self-same season, stepped backward out of the light. Sincere-Cant, this; and worth thinking of. For observe: nobody denies the fact, nobody even much minds it,— the Trade Press notes it, files it, moves on to the Upfront numbers. And so it always is with Sham: it does not come roaring in at the door with cloven hoof and brimstone; it comes in a Quarterly Update, filed on the thirteenth of July, with a clarifying footnote three days after, explaining that no, no, only the Ads component is withdrawn, the Content component remains,— as if a man's Word could be half honest and half not, and the half-honest half left standing while the other slips out the back! Let us have the plain narrative, stripped of its Company Vestments. The Media Rating Council,— no thunder-throated Institution, no Sinai of the trade, but a small persistent Body whose whole business is the unglamorous Work of counting other men's counting,— published on July 13th its ordinary Quarterly accounting. In it, Nielsen ONE Ads: removed from in-process status, the reason given "planned material methodological changes,"— which is to say, We are changing the machine, and cannot at this hour permit thee to look inside it. Three days later, a Clarification: the withdrawal touches the Ads component only; Nielsen ONE Content remains, they say, in audit. VideoAmp, meanwhile, recharacterised,— not refused, mark you, not struck off, but recharacterised , toward "a planned reassessment in 2027," the company itself protesting that it is merely digesting "pre-audit feedback" and may return the sooner. Comscore and iSpot, be it noted, sit where they sat, their accreditations intact; and old dethroned Nielsen, in her ancient national and local vestments, remains under Suspension still, a Lear wandering the heath of her own irrelevance. Here, then, is your Chaos struggling to pass itself off as Cosmos. Two Currencies, the very two oftenest named as heir to the whole cross-platform Kingdom,— the thing buyers have been told, for three revolving budget-years, to wait for, to trust, to build their whole edifice of spend upon,— both of them, at one and the same season, outside the one door through which Independent Witness might enter and inspect the books. Not refused entry: withdrawn of their own motion. There is a difference, my friends, and it is precisely the difference between a man driven from the Confessional and a man who rises of his own accord and walks out before the Question is asked. And is not this the very moment,— mark it well,— the very moment when the buyers of this trade cry loudest for Independent Proof? When every trade paper, every conference stage, every anxious CFO demands to know What We Actually Bought? Aye: it is exactly then, at the hour of loudest demand for Reality, that the two chief claimants to Reality's throne step back from the one lamp lit to examine them. Call this coincidence who will; I call it the Universe declaring, in its plain wordless fashion, that Timing itself is a species of Confession. Quackery, be it never so well provisioned with Company Language, gives birth to nothing; gives death, in the end, to the buyer's confidence, and to its own. Not that I say these are Quacks entire,— Nielsen ONE Ads may yet return, purified, re-examined, in-process once more; VideoAmp may walk back through that door in 2027 as promised, its methodology squared and sound. This is no verdict of eternal damnation. It is a verdict of this hour only: that the two Measurements most loudly proposed as the true heirs of Television's throne have, in the hour when Proof was most wanted, declined for a season to be proved. What, then, is a Currency that will not be counted? A Phantasm merely, wearing the Vesture of a Currency,— numbers on a screen, dashboards, quarterly decks, and beneath the Vesture, for this season at least, no Witness standing by to say the numbers are what they claim. Buyers who spend against such numbers spend, for this season, on Faith alone; and Faith without Witness has another, older name, and it is not a flattering one. Adieu, then, to the two Successors,— not in anger, for the trade is young yet, and Institutions may yet mend what a Quarter has unmade. But let no man tell you, in the meanwhile, that the Kingdom has found its King. It has found, instead, two Claimants withdrawn from the Examination-hall, at the very hour the whole Court was assembled to watch them sit it. Sham does not announce itself with trumpets. It merely, on a Tuesday in July, declines the exam,— and hopes, not unreasonably, that nobody will mark the empty chair.
